name: Grey Beige
lede: Grey Beige is a light, greyed tan, the color of undyed wool and dry dust, named by blending two neutral words.

sections.title: Two neutrals in one
sections.body:
The earliest record in our sources is the German RAL system of 1927, and ISCC-NBS later places the swatch among light grayish yellowish browns [1]. The books read say nothing about the name itself, beyond one mention of gray, beige and brown tones in a discussion of Rembrandt's 1632 *Anatomy Lesson of Doctor Tulp*, where they accompany black and white [2]. That is a description of a painting, not of a named color.

Beige is itself an old French word for undyed wool, so the name says, in effect, a greyer beige [1]. Its near neighbors are [[beige]] and [[grey]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is one of the commonest colors in paintings: 2,644 of 23,781 pieces contain it, 11.1 per cent, more than 95 per cent of named colors [3]. In most of those it is a hidden color, neither the lightest nor the darkest [3]. It peaks in the 1200s, at 20.4 per cent of 142 paintings, which is probably the tone of aged panels and silk [3]. Jan Wijnants leans on it most, in 5 of 13 works [3]. It often shares a canvas with [[dusty-sepia]] and [[sandust]] [3]. These are photographs of aged paintings, so the grey in it is partly time [3].

origin.named_after: beige, the old word for undyed wool, made greyer
